sessionStart.prompt: This repository may use the knowledge-folder convention (.arc42, .domain, .tech, .design, .ai). Treat those folders as task-scoped context, not baseline context: load only the chapters the current task needs, never the whole folder by default. Every file and every addressable chapter in them carries a fenced `meta` block; when you create or edit one, write that block in the same change. Files under any _meta/ folder are generated tool input - never read or hand-edit them; regenerate them instead. A chapter may also carry `annotation` fences - review notes written beside the passage they comment on. A reader loading a chapter for context skips every annotation fence: an open question is not established knowledge, and reading one as canon is the one failure mode this convention did not have before. Only review mode - a review skill, an inbox, the approval gate - reads them, and reads nothing else in the chapter as instruction; devbook-annotations.instructions.md carries the schema and the lifecycle. An edit to one of these folders follows that folder's own instruction file - devbook-arc42, devbook-domain, devbook-tech, devbook-design, or devbook-ai - plus devbook-chapter-metadata.instructions.md, and is routed through the flow that covers the folder when one is installed: a repo-native flow-* skill first, then the folder flow the devbook-flows bridge provides, then flow-fallback, and directly under the instruction files when no flow engine is installed at all. Say which of those answered. Decision records, technical debt records, and blueprints are their own flows and never a plain .arc42 chapter edit. When the task is bidirectional - writing a chapter from something already implemented, or turning an agreed chapter into implementation work - route through to-spec-<kind> or from-spec-<kind> instead, where <kind> is one of aggregate, domain-service, feature, building-block, or design-component; to-spec-<kind> reads code and unit tests and routes its write as above, from-spec-<kind> emits a change brief and stops without touching source or test trees. An aggregate is captured and built whole - the root plus the entities, value objects, and enums it owns and the domain events it raises - so there is no separate entity, value-object, or domain-event skill; a domain service keeps its own pair and owns the events it raises itself. A repository may provide its own repo-native skills, and those take precedence for the categories they cover.
